Are Interest Rates Higher?—In this section, I test whether borrowers in inflated 
transactions are more likely to pay higher mortgage rates. The sample used consists 
of 57,788 mortgages in which lenders voluntarily report annualized percentage rates 
(APRs) post-2003.28
The tests of the relation between seller hints, foreclosure, and mortgage prices is 
presented in Table 5, columns 3, 6, and 7. Column 3 repeats the foreclosure likeli-
hood tests (from columns 1 and 2) for the sample that is used to study interest rates. 
The results show that the likelihood of foreclosure for highly leveraged borrow-
ers is statistically weak (t = 0.8 to 1.2) due to the small sample size; however, the 
coefficients are large and economically significant (the likelihood of foreclosure is 
higher by 1.3 percent (9.2 percent) for those who, with an LTV of 95–100 percent 
(> 100 percent), buy properties that include sellers’ hints relative to those who do 
not). Columns 6 and 7 show that borrowers with LTV of 95–100 percent who buy 
properties with sellers’ hints pay interest rates that are higher by 0.05–0.27 percent; 
further, these rates are not monotonic and therefore do not seem to reflect the risk 
that increases with leverage.

prior achievement, we included learners’ prior achievement (high-

4.3. Rapid-guessing behavior
Our descriptive data in Table 2 show that RPs reduced students’
tendency to engage in RGB to a substantial extent. RGB rates increased
with item positions, but text-picture items were on average always less
aﬀected by RGB than text-only items.
